title: "Grandma, I Want To Be," by Felecia Williams, Read Aloud
fulltitle: "Grandma, I Want To Be," by Felecia Williams, Read Aloud
description:
"Grandma, I Want To Be" is a fun and easy read following a little girls as she tells her supportive grandmother everything she wants to be when she grows up. Her quest is to find the right passion and it is not an easy decision! She loves race cars, science, baking, teaching, and more. Will she ever be able to choose just one thing? 

When there are many things you love to do, it is okay to say, "I want to be everything!" And grandmothers can help grandkids dream big and go far.

This book celebrates the special bond a child has with their grandma.

If you'd like to purchase this book, please visit:

https://www.amazon.com/Grandma-Want-Be-Felecia-Williams/dp/0578618591

description:
"No Hair, Don't Care" is the story of how a mother and daughter learn to cope with the side effects of chemotherapy and hair loss in particular. title: Lailah's Lunchbox - A Ramadan Story
fulltitle: Lailah's Lunchbox - A Ramadan Story
description:
"Lailah is in a new school in a new country, thousands of miles from her old home, and missing her old friends. When Ramadan begins, she is excited that she is finally old enough to participate in the fasting but worried that her classmates won’t understand why she doesn’t join them in the lunchroom.

Lailah solves her problem with help from the school librarian and her teacher and in doing so learns that she can make new friends who respect her beliefs. This gentle, moving story from first-time author Reem Faruqi comes to life in Lea Lyon’s vibrant illustrations. Lyon uses decorative arabesque borders on intermittent spreads to contrast the ordered patterns of Islamic observances with the unbounded rhythms of American school days."

'In an African village live seven brothers who make family life miserable with their constant fighting. When their father dies, he leaves an unusual will: by sundown, the brothers must make gold out of seven spools of thread. If they fail, they will be turned out as beggars.

'What is a family? 

Once, it was said to be a father, mother, boy, girl, cat and dog living in a house with a garden. But as times have changed, families have changed too, and now there are almost as many kinds of families as colors of the rainbow: from a mom and dad or single parent to two mums or two dads, from a mixed-race family to children with different moms and dads, to families with a disabled member. 

Mary Hoffman, the author of "Amazing Grace", takes a look through children's eyes at the wide varieties of family life: from homes, food, ways of celebrating, schools and holidays to getting around, jobs and housework, from extended families, languages and hobbies to pets and family trees - and she concludes that, for most people, their own family is the best one of all! With Ros Asquith's delightful pictures, this book takes a fresh, optimistic look at families of today.'

Chapter 2. Pooh Goes Visiting and Gets Into a Tight Place 
READ ALOUD


Created by A A Milne in 1924, Winnie the Pooh first appeared in a collection of stories in the London Evening News and later in his own titular book in 1926. He was based on the toy bear by the same name, bought for his son, Christopher Robin. Yes, THAT Christopher Robin, along with Christopher's other stuffed animals, Piglet, Kanga, Roo, Tigger and Eeyore. Owl and Rabbit were later created for the book, and Gopher who appears in the Disney anthology movie, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh," (1977) was made for the movie - hence his line and play on words, "I'm not in the book!"

'Before writing Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne was already a successful writer who wrote for the British humor magazine "Punch", had published a mystery novel and was a playwright. Milne began writing poetry for children and later compiled his first verses for publishing, and though his publishers were initially hesitant to publish children's poetry, the poetry collection When We Were Very Young (1924) was a success. It was through this project he met and first collaborated with illustrator E H Shepard.

Among the characters in When We Were Very Young was a teddy bear that Milne modelled after one belonging to his son, Christopher Robin. With the book's success, Shepard encouraged Milne to write stories about Milne's young son  and his stuffed toys, especially the bear he called "Winnie-the-Pooh". Christopher got the name "Winnie" from a bear at the London Zoo, Winnipeg. "Pooh" was the name of a swan they nicknamed while at a stay at the children's hospital.

Milne used Christopher and his toys as inspiration for a series of short stories, which were compiled and published as Winnie-the-Pooh. The model for Pooh remained the bear belonging to Shepard's son. The books of course went on to become a huge success and are now more commonly associated with the Disney franchise.  Penguin Books has called When We Were Very Young, Winnie-the-Pooh, Now We Are Six, and The House At Pooh Corner "the basis of the entire Pooh canon."

On a side note, Winnie the Pooh was HUGE in the late 70's and was everywhere you looked in a Sears & Roebuck, which to translate those last few words to the younger generation, if Amazon was an indoor theme park. But to go on, Winnie the Pooh was huge in my childhood and I had a little doll that had a music box inside that when you wound it, it played the Winnie the Pooh theme. I slept with that doll just about every night until I was six and replaced it with  Gizmo from Gremlins. Signs of the times. All the same, that little yellow bear meant a lot. 

It was a marker of my childhood, and a memory that reminded me, 'whatever happens to us on the way, in that enchanted place on the top of the Forest, a little child and their Bear will always be playing.'

'What is a family? 

Once, it was said to be a father, mother, boy, girl, cat and dog living in a house with a garden. But as times have changed, families have changed too, and now there are almost as many kinds of families as colors of the rainbow: from a mom and dad or single parent to two mums or two dads, from a mixed-race family to children with different moms and dads, to families with a disabled member. 

Mary Hoffman, the author of "Amazing Grace", takes a look through children's eyes at the wide varieties of family life: from homes, food, ways of celebrating, schools and holidays to getting around, jobs and housework, from extended families, languages and hobbies to pets and family trees - and she concludes that, for most people, their own family is the best one of all! With Ros Asquith's delightful pictures, this book takes a fresh, optimistic look at families of today.'

Chapter 2. Pooh Goes Visiting and Gets Into a Tight Place 
READ ALOUD


Created by A A Milne in 1924, Winnie the Pooh first appeared in a collection of stories in the London Evening News and later in his own titular book in 1926. He was based on the toy bear by the same name, bought for his son, Christopher Robin. Yes, THAT Christopher Robin, along with Christopher's other stuffed animals, Piglet, Kanga, Roo, Tigger and Eeyore. Owl and Rabbit were later created for the book, and Gopher who appears in the Disney anthology movie, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh," (1977) was made for the movie - hence his line and play on words, "I'm not in the book!"

'Before writing Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne was already a successful writer who wrote for the British humor magazine "Punch", had published a mystery novel and was a playwright. Milne began writing poetry for children and later compiled his first verses for publishing, and though his publishers were initially hesitant to publish children's poetry, the poetry collection When We Were Very Young (1924) was a success. It was through this project he met and first collaborated with illustrator E H Shepard.

Among the characters in When We Were Very Young was a teddy bear that Milne modelled after one belonging to his son, Christopher Robin. With the book's success, Shepard encouraged Milne to write stories about Milne's young son  and his stuffed toys, especially the bear he called "Winnie-the-Pooh". Christopher got the name "Winnie" from a bear at the London Zoo, Winnipeg. "Pooh" was the name of a swan they nicknamed while at a stay at the children's hospital.

Milne used Christopher and his toys as inspiration for a series of short stories, which were compiled and published as Winnie-the-Pooh. The model for Pooh remained the bear belonging to Shepard's son. The books of course went on to become a huge success and are now more commonly associated with the Disney franchise.  Penguin Books has called When We Were Very Young, Winnie-the-Pooh, Now We Are Six, and The House At Pooh Corner "the basis of the entire Pooh canon."

On a side note, Winnie the Pooh was HUGE in the late 70's and was everywhere you looked in a Sears & Roebuck, which to translate those last few words to the younger generation, if Amazon was an indoor theme park. But to go on, Winnie the Pooh was huge in my childhood and I had a little doll that had a music box inside that when you wound it, it played the Winnie the Pooh theme. I slept with that doll just about every night until I was six and replaced it with  Gizmo from Gremlins. Signs of the times. All the same, that little yellow bear meant a lot. 

It was a marker of my childhood, and a memory that reminded me, 'whatever happens to us on the way, in that enchanted place on the top of the Forest, a little child and their Bear will always be playing.'

description:
A Peacock Among Pigeons
written by Tyler Curry
illustrated by Clarione Gutierrez

Read Aloud by
Dr Francois Clemmons
(Officer Clemmons of "Mr Rogers Neighborhood")

Read by Dr Francois Clemmons (OFFICER CLEMMONS of Mr Rogers Neighborhood), in this new take on The Ugly Duckling"  -- or in this case, The Fierce Pigeon -- author Tyler Curry tells the story of Peter the peacock who doesn't know how it happened, but found himself growing up in a flock of pigeons. Surrounded by a world of grey, he found himself feeling less than his peers and was embarrassed by his feathers. After he fails to blend in, he decides that it's time to learn to fly on his own. Along the way, he meets new bird friends from all different flocks that teach him a lesson he will never forget.

A Peacock Among Pigeons is an LGBT-themed hardback children's book that tells the tale of learning how to stand out when you can't fit in. This children's story teaches the importance of celebrating our differences and learning to love the feathers you live in.

Published by Mascot Books, 2015.

The Boy Who Said Wow
by Todd Boss

Inspired by the beautiful true story of a nonverbal boy moved to speech at his first Mozart concert, this picture book is a testament to the power of art and the boundless joy it can bring.

When Grandfather comes to take his grandson to a concert, Ronan is quiet as they leave the house, quiet in the car, and quiet at the concert hall. But when the performance is over and the beautiful music fades out at last, Ronan opens his mouth…and lets out a great big WOW!

Not any old WOW, but Ronan’s very first WOW! That one word fills up the hearts of Ronan’s family, the musicians, the audience, and—when the recording goes viral—the world. A beautiful story for ALL families of ALL ages that can see the true power of music, family, and a child's wonder.

What a lovely afternoon, says mother. Shall we go to the park? Ronan is quiet. Suddenly, grandfather bursts through the door. Let's go to a concert. A risk, says mother. A challenge, says father. An adventure, cries grandfather. Ronan is quiet as he gets into the car. He is quiet as they leave the sleepy countryside. The city is noisy. Grandfather is noisy, too. He talks and talks and talks. But Ronan is quiet all the way to Symphony Hall. Some children are born noisy, but Ronin was born quiet. Some days he hardly says a word. What goes on in his head, do you suppose? Only Ronin knows. What a fantastic concert hall, says Ronan's grandfather as they take their seats. Ronin is quiet as the musicians come on stage. Ronin is quiet as the lights go down. Everyone is quiet now. The music is about to begin. And then it [Music] does. The darker instruments sound cool and frightening. The lighter instruments sound warm and friendly. Together they sound like a sky full of stars. Now the music is done. Everything is silent. The stars fade away. Then Ronan's mouth opens and out comes a great big. This wow isn't just any old wow. It's Ronan's first wow. It fills up Ronan's whole face. It fills up the hearts of all the people in the audience. It fills up the whole concert hall. Everybody laughs. Then everybody claps. They are clapping for the orchestra. And they are clapping for Ronin, too. Ronan is quiet all the way home. Ronan is quiet as he's tucked into bed. "Wow," whispers mother. "Wow," whispers father. "Sh, quiet now. Ronin may still be listening." This story really happened on May 5th, 2019 at Boston's Symphony Hall. A 9-year-old boy named Ronan Matine broke the silence after a performance of Mozart's Masonic funeral music by the Hanel and Aiden Society with a wow that echoed throughout the hall and inspired laughter, cheers, and applause. Ronin is non-verbal, which means he usually doesn't speak much, but that night he seemed to speak for everyone in the audience. And his wow was caught on a radio recording that was heard around the world. [Music]

written by Naaz Khan

The dala dala rumbles and roars as Musa and Dada drive off to the shore—but the bus stops for multiple detours: “Do you need a ride? It’s hotter than peppers out there in the sun! Come in, there’s room for everyone!”

Why can't I love sport and dancing and trains and ponies and glitter and engines and planes? Why must I choose and exclude all the rest? I love choosing both because both is the best. And now it is time for the greatest event. The school dance is here. The invites been sent. I'm ready to rock and I'm feeling cute. My mom made my skirt and my dad made my suit. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en My Brother Charlie. Written by Holly Robinson Pete and Ryan Elizabeth Pete. Pictures by Shane W. Evans. We've always been together. Even in mommy's tummy. My twin brother Charlie and me. We still share lots of things. Curly hair and brown eyes. How much we love hot chocolate with marshmallows, our dog Harriet, rolling in the grass, music, football, and names that start with the letter C. Callie and Charlie. But being twins doesn't make us exactly the same. I'm 2 minutes younger than Charlie. I can stare for hours at the Big Dipper and the moon. and I love to talk. Charlie is skinnier and goofier than me. He hates math. When he looks at the sky, he finds jets and helicopters. And sometimes my brother gets very quiet. When we were babies, I pointed out flowers and cats and fireflies. I snuggled and giggled with mommy on dark nights and told mommy again and again how much I love her. But Charlie was different. He wouldn't play with me or kiss mommy's cheeks when she hugged him. And he didn't say, "I love you." Seems those words were locked deep inside my brother. Everyone told mommy not to worry. He's just being a boy, they said. But mommy knew there was something different about Charlie. I knew it, too. As we grew older, Mommy watched Charlie very carefully. She and I could see he was struggling. Then, Mommy discovered that Charlie's brain works in a special way because Charlie has autism. It's harder for Charlie to make friends or show his feelings or stay safe. One doctor even told mommy that Charlie would never say, "I love you." That made mommy and me saddest of all. I have learned from Charlie that love doesn't always come from what you say. It can also come from what you do. And so we do right by Charlie. We love Charlie strong. We watch over him with the might of angels. We have to. When Charlie wants something, nothing stops him. Even when it's dangerous, and there are days when it's hard to be Charlie's sister. Sometimes he can ruin the best playdates. Other times he seems so far away, like when he won't look at me or speak or play. I wish I could crawl inside Charlie's world to move things around for him and for me. I know Charlie wants to be in my world, fitting in, making friends, having fun, and laughing. There are good times with Charlie, too. When Charlie looks right at me and welcomes me with his smile. He lets me touch his face. He laughs when we lock fingers in a holding hands game. That's Charlie's I love you, said in the silly ways we play together. Charlie is good at so much. He knows the names of all the American presidents. He's a fish in the water. He has a special way with animals, especially Harriet. When Harriet and Charlie are together, there's even more I love you. Said in the way only Charlie can when he gets Harriet to sit, run, or listen. Charlie's got a mind that tests things. shoelaces, paper clips, apples, pine cones, and he enjoys sharing. He likes to show off his shell collection, his new sneakers, and how well he plays Itsybitsy Spider on the piano. Charlie likes to share how sweet he is and how much he cares about other people. When I fall off my bike or bump my head, Charlie comes running. He always makes my hurts feel better with the caring that comes from his eyes. Sometimes when Charlie can find the words when they unlock themselves from inside him, he does say, "I love you." I will always remember the first time I heard him say it. So clear and kind. So, Charlie, I banged my toe hard and cried. There was my brother patting my back, saying over and over again, "Don't cry, Callie! I love you. Charlie has autism, but autism doesn't have Charlie. If you ever get to meet my brother, you'll feel lucky to be his friend. He won't care if you have the coolest sneakers or if you're the best at sports. He'll just like you for who you really are. That's Charlie. I'm blessed to be Charlie's sister and to share so much. I count my Charlie blessings every day. The Boy Who Said Wow
by Todd Boss

Inspired by the beautiful true story of a nonverbal boy moved to speech at his first Mozart concert, this picture book is a testament to the power of art and the boundless joy it can bring.

When Grandfather comes to take his grandson to a concert, Ronan is quiet as they leave the house, quiet in the car, and quiet at the concert hall. But when the performance is over and the beautiful music fades out at last, Ronan opens his mouth…and lets out a great big WOW!

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Leo's Lunchbox written by Raphael G. Waro and illustrated by Tama Grooms. A baloney sandwich. Not again. Leo didn't like bologoney sandwiches. Yet, this was the fourth time this week mom packed one for a school lunch. Bologna with mustard, bologna with mayo, bologoney with cheese, lettuce, and tomato. Sometimes she would fry it until it bubbled up in the pan. But it was still bologoney. "For now, it's all we can afford," Mom said. As Leo sat there in the school cafeteria, barely nibbling on the sandwich, Pete laughed while leaning over to him. "Hey, Leo, what's that you're eating?" "Another bologoney sandwich." Pete was a big kid with a big mouth, and he was always teasing Leo about his lunch. Phil joined in with the teasing. "A baloney sandwich? Leave him alone," said Joanna. And what if I don't? asked Pete. Before she could answer, the bell rang and it was time to go back to class. In class, it was hard for Leo to focus on his schoolwork. He was tired. Tired of eating the same old sandwich, tired of being teased by Pete. And because his lunch was so small, he was still a little hungry and a little sad. He looked over at his friend Andy. Andy looked tired, too. His family couldn't even afford baloney. He'd had a breadand butter sandwich for lunch. It felt like the school day would never end. Finally, the bell rang and Leo, his tummy rumbling, got on the big yellow school bus and went home. "How was school today?" Mom asked over dinner. It was okay. Leo said he didn't really want to talk about it, so he shoveled down his fried baloney and went straight to his room. He said his prayers and went to sleep. When he woke up the next morning, there was a shiny lunchbox sitting in the kitchen. "Good morning," Mom said. "Guess what? Last night after you went to sleep, I found out I got a new job. I ran to the secondhand store and I bought you this lunchbox. When I walked up into the store, it looked like it glowed. Anyway, I think you'll like your new lunch, but promise me you won't open it until lunchtime at school. Could that mean that Leo wasn't going to get a bologn sandwich? Did mom buy something special when she went out last night? When lunchtime came, Leo rushed to open his lunchbox. He couldn't wait to see what mom had packed. No bologoney sandwich. In fact, inside were two slices of pizza, and they were still warm. As Leo was about to eat his pizza, he noticed his friend Andy had no lunch at all that day. Not even a bread and butter sandwich. Leo really wanted both slices, but decided to give one to Andy and keep the other for himself. When he finished eating his one slice of pizza, he looked into his lunchbox and saw an orange, his favorite fruit. That's when Manuel looked over. Manuel was new to Leo's school. Sometimes he spoke in Spanish and struggled with English, but he was great in math and helped Leo understand fractions and multiplication. Leo reached for the orange, thinking he might share it with Manuel. And to his amazement, next to the orange was a third slice of pizza. Wow, I guess I didn't see it before, he thought. Hey, Manuel, want half of this slice of pizza? Leo asked with a twinkle in his eye. Sure, thanks buddy. Leo took the dull plastic knife mom had placed in the lunchbox and began to cut the pizza in half. But as he cut it in half, each slice doubled in size. One slice was now the slice of two. too much for one kid to eat. So he cut each slice again. One became two, two became four. He kept cutting and the pizza kept growing. Four became eight, eight became 16. "Wow, this is amazing," said Manuel. Other kids began to gather, so Leo began passing the pizza around. It seemed the more he gave, the more he had. So he kept reaching into that shiny lunchbox, not really to see what he could get, but to see what he could give. Giving to others felt really good. He reached for the orange that he had almost forgotten about because of all the excitement and handed it to Joanna. He loved oranges, but she loved them, too. Besides, he remembered that Joanna had stood up for him when Pete and Phil had teased him yesterday. "Hey, Joanna, take this orange." "Thanks," she said. "But you keep it. You love oranges." "It's okay," he said. "It's a thank you for standing up for me." "I tell you what," she said. "Let's split it." Leo reached back into that magical lunchbox and handed her a plastic knife. And as she cut the orange in half, each slice doubled. One slice was now two. Two became four. She kept cutting and the orange slices kept coming. Four became eight. Eight became 16. So she started sharing them around just like Leo had with the pizza. And it turned into a party. Kids were eating, singing, dancing, sharing. Maria had chips. Nate had dip. And others did, too. So they poured all the chips into one big bowl, and all the dip into another. Chips and dip for everyone. With all that pizza and dip and all those oranges and chips, Leo was thirsty. So he reached into the magical lunchbox and pulled out the magical blue thermos. He poured himself some juice, but there was more. So he poured himself another cup. And still there was more. So he poured Joanna a cup. And still there was more. So he poured Maria and then Nate a cup and still there was more. The more he poured, the more he had. The more he gave, the more he received. Juice and chips and dip, pizza and oranges, singing, dancing, sharing. There was such commotion and so much excitement that Pete couldn't take it anymore. He slowly came over and Phil followed him. And with his hand shaking, he asked Leo, "May I?" No way, said Joanna, guarding the oranges. It's okay, Leo said to her. We have more than enough for everyone. Then he turned to Pete and Phil. Go ahead, he said, and sharing still felt good. Actually, somehow it felt even better. Hey, Annie said, sipping a cup of juice. Thanks for sharing your lunch with me. It's the first time I've been full at school all year. Leo smiled. Me, too, he said. Do you think your lunchbox will keep giving us pizza? Leo shrugged. I don't know, he said. But maybe it doesn't have to. Maybe it taught us all we needed to learn. And Leo was right. After that day, no one at his school ever went to class hungry again. Hey there, friendly readers. "Someone Just Like You"
written by Helen Docherty
Illustrated by David Roberts

From celebrated picture book author Helen Docherty and the bestselling illustrator of the Questioneers series, David Roberts, comes a vitally important picture book encouraging empathy by showing we’re more similar than different.

Somewhere in this world, there is someone just like you, who finds the same things funny and who laughs the way you do. If they needed you, would you help them? This moving call to action reminds kids through lyrical, rhyming text and stunning illustrations that people share more similarities than differences and that kindness is doable and actionable, even when you’re small.

Published by Simon & Schuster Books for Young Readers, 2024.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Someone just like you. Written by Helen Dory and pictures by David Roberts. Somewhere in this world, there is someone just like you who finds the same things funny and who laughs the way you do. You may speak a different language. You may have a different name. On the outside, you look different, but your feelings are the same. The same things make you giggle. The same things make you mad. The same things make you curious. The same things make you sad. The same things make you happy. The same things make you scared. But you'd both feel so much better if you knew that someone cared. If this someone needed shelter or a place to sleep at night. If they'd have to leave their home because they didn't want to fight. If you saw them feeling sad because they'd left their friends behind, would you be the one to hug them when they needed someone kind? Would you share the things you had with them and help them feel at home? Would you find them things they needed like a toothbrush or a comb? Would you listen to their story? Would you tell them yours as well? Would you talk about the things you love, a book, a favorite smell? Would you help them feel safe again and chase their fears away? Would you find a way to make them smile when skies were looking gray? Somewhere in this world, there is someone just like you. Perhaps one day you'll meet them. They would love to meet you, too.
